name: Conversion: Faith and Repentance

objectives.text: Identify faith as trusting Jesus to save us, using a Bible account in which someone trusts Jesus
Name repentance as turning away from sin and turning toward God
Recall Jesus' first gospel preaching that people must repent and believe
Retell the account of Zacchaeus and describe how he turned from his sin to follow Jesus
Explain that faith and repentance always go together in the gospel call
Recite the Westminster Shorter Catechism answers that define faith in Jesus Christ and repentance unto life
Describe the three parts of saving faith as knowledge, assent, and trust
Explain the parts of repentance unto life as seeing sin, grieving over it, hating it, and turning to God with a purpose of new obedience
Distinguish godly sorrow from worldly sorrow by comparing the responses of Peter and Judas after their sins
Compare true saving faith with mere intellectual belief using biblical examples of false or shallow faith
Analyze Psalm 51 as a model of repentance by identifying its confession of sin, appeal to mercy, and resolve to obey
Examine how the apostolic sermons in Acts call hearers to repent and believe and describe how the hearers responded
Analyze faith and repentance as two inseparable sides of one conversion and explain why neither exists without the other
Explain that saving faith rests on Christ alone as its object rather than on the strength or quality of the believer's faith
Explain from Scripture that faith and repentance are gifts worked by the Holy Spirit rather than human achievements
Explain the Reformed teaching that repentance continues throughout the Christian life as the dying of the old self and the rising of the new
Explain why the Reformed confessions teach that repentance is no satisfaction for sin and yet is necessary for every sinner
Prepare a clear explanation of the gospel call to repent and believe that is faithful to Scripture and suited to a younger audience
Defend the Reformed teaching that faith is the instrument that receives Christ and his righteousness rather than a meritorious work
Analyze how James 2 and Romans 4 together show that living faith is never alone but bears fruit in obedience
Evaluate easy-believism and works-righteousness as distortions of the biblical teaching on faith and repentance
Compare the Reformed account of repentance with the Roman Catholic sacrament of penance
Compare the Reformed view that faith and repentance flow from regeneration with the Arminian view of faith as preceding new birth
Compose a biblical and confessional account of conversion as the sinner's Spirit-wrought response of faith and repentance to God's grace

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (faith as trust, repentance as turning, knowledge-assent-trust, repentance unto life, faith versus mere belief, two sides of conversion, faith resting on Christ, gift of the Spirit, instrumental role, distortions, final synthesis). Merged the separate gift and Spirit objectives into one. Dropped the filler 'saved by believing not earning' and the justification-construction objective, which belong to the Justification sibling, keeping only the instrumental role of faith. Reworded 'Apply the call to repent and believe' so it no longer asks for a personal response and instead has students trace the call in Acts and prepare an explanation of it. Added Bible narratives (Zacchaeus, Peter and Judas), Mark 1:15, catechism recitation, Psalm 51 as a model of repentance, ongoing repentance, repentance as no satisfaction, James 2 with Romans 4, comparison with Roman Catholic penance, and the Reformed versus Arminian ordering. Corrected confession citations to standard names and numbers.
